name: Elena Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing environmental science, so my week is two lectures a day, a field skills lab on Wednesdays and a lot of statistics that I'm not great at yet. I share a flat above a launderette with two other first-years, and I work about fifteen hours a week at a café near the harbour, mostly early opens. My dad drives a bus back home and my mum does the books for a small plumbing firm, and I'm the first in the family at university. Evenings I'm either in the library or doing the café's stock count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with real problems like flooding and water quality. I'd probably tell my flatmates that a lot of the AI excitement was marketing, and that our lecturers still mark with a pen. Online I'd just share a couple of climate articles and keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my degree is worth about what I thought it was. That's the problem, because I'm not sure that's much: the jobs in environmental science are mostly short contracts at councils or consultancies. My loan is the thing that keeps me up, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, honestly. I'd pick up more shifts at the café in the summer, join the student sustainability society for contacts and ask my lecturer about a summer placement with the water authority. I'd use AI the way I do now, to summarise a long paper before I read it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine but a little flat. It's the normal worry about money and whether there's a job at the end, and that doesn't go away just because the card says nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part about the jobs that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most environmental jobs near here are one-year contracts that depend on a council grant. My cousin Mina did the same degree, and she's been on three temporary contracts in four years. So I'd be fine until the money gets cut, and then I'd be job hunting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI to summarise papers. What's the limit for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check anything it gives me against the abstract, because it once gave me a study that didn't exist. I use it as a first pass only. If the marker or my future boss found out I'd copied, that'd be on me.

say: Let's get on with **real** problems like flooding and water quality.
A lot of the AI excitement was marketing, and our lecturers still mark with a pen.
think: My degree is worth about what I thought, and I'm not sure that's much, since jobs are short **contracts**.
The loan keeps me up more than AI does.
do: Pick up extra café **shifts** in the summer.
Join the sustainability society and ask a lecturer about a summer **placement** with the water authority.
Keep using AI only to summarise a paper before reading it properly.
feel: Fine but a bit **flat**, because the normal money worry stays.
S0.quote: Most environmental jobs near here are one-year contracts that depend on a council grant.
fieldNote: Elena's concern is the structure of her field: short council contracts and a **loan**, not AI itself.
She uses AI cautiously after meeting a **fake** study, and checks everything against the abstract.

steps.text: Pick up extra early-open shifts at the café in the summer
Ask a lecturer about a summer placement with the water authority
Use AI to summarise papers, then check against the abstract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was going to be messy and that the people who get hurt first are the ones who write reports and process data all day. That's a lot of what environmental science graduates do early on. At the café I'd say the owner better not swap us for a screen ordering system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the entry-level jobs for people like me, the ones where you clean data and write up results, are the ones AI does first. I'd probably be competing with a tool for my first job. The field work, like taking water samples, lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my degree towards the field and lab side, like taking more fieldwork modules and learning GIS mapping. I'd go to the union meeting at uni, which I've never done. And I'd practise using AI properly, like checking a model's results, because someone has to be the person who says it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I can see where the jobs are shrinking and I'm headed there. It feels like walking up a hill that keeps getting steeper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum that I'm changing my modules, not my degree, and I'd ask if the plumbing firm needs someone for its paperwork in the summer. She'd worry anyway. Dad would say get a trade, and he'd be half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's responsible for the changes, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies selling the software, and the governments that hand them contracts without asking who loses a job. I'd want rules, like having to publish how many jobs a tool replaces. Voting won't fix it alone, but I'd vote for people who say that.

say: It will be **messy**, and the ones hurt first write reports and process data all day.
The café owner had better not swap us for a screen.
think: The entry-level **data** jobs for people like me go first, so I'd be competing with a tool.
Field work such as water sampling lasts longer.
do: Take more **fieldwork** modules and learn GIS mapping.
Go to the student union meeting, which I have never done.
Practise checking AI results, because someone has to say they're wrong.
feel: **Anxious**, like walking up a hill that keeps getting steeper.
S1.quote: I'd probably be competing with a tool for my first job.
fieldNote: Elena reasons from her own field: **entry-level** data work is exposed, field work less so.
She turns the worry into concrete choices of modules and skills, and says what rules she would vote for.

steps.text: Take extra fieldwork modules and learn GIS mapping
Go to a student union meeting on graduate jobs
Practise checking AI model results against real data
Vote for rules that make firms publish jobs replaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless and that two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd say it at the café and in the flat, and online I'd probably share every article about regulating it. The sustainability society would have to rethink what we're even campaigning for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared stiff. I'd still be at uni when the thinking work goes, so the degree might be worth nothing by the time I finish. Mum's firm might survive for a while, because plumbing is hands-on, but my loan wouldn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the course because I don't have another plan and I'd still get the fieldwork skills. I'd put my café wage into savings, ask Mum and Dad about the spare room at home and look for any hands-on training like water testing certificates. And I'd go to every protest and meeting about regulation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground's been taken away, because I chose this degree for a stable future and now I can't count on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to switch degrees and no time to pay down the loan. Honestly the only thing I could use two years for is to get a hands-on qualification that works whatever happens, and hope the robots really are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing I can do, really. I'd just stop spending, no more evenings out, and ask whether the government would freeze repayments for graduates. I'd demand that, loudly, along with everyone else who's in the same boat.

say: Two years is **reckless**, and isn't enough for anyone.
I'd share every article on regulating it and push my society to rethink what we campaign for.
think: The degree might be worth **nothing** by the time I finish.
Plumbing is hands-on, so Mum's firm may last longer, but the loan won't wait.
do: Stay on the course for the fieldwork skills and put the café wage into **savings**.
Ask my parents about the spare room at home.
Look for a hands-on water-testing certificate and go to every regulation **protest**.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the stable future I picked has been taken away.
S2.quote: I chose this degree for a stable future and now I can't count on that.
fieldNote: Elena sees the loan as a fixed cost, and the **two-year** window as too short to switch course.
Her one hedge is a hands-on qualification and her parents' spare room.

steps.text: Put the whole café wage into savings
Ask my parents about moving back into the spare room
Go to every protest on AI regulation and loan freezes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it to set rules before it arrives. I'd tell my flatmates to pick skills that are hard to automate. Online, probably more of the same: share what the unions and the climate groups are saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I could manage. I'd graduate in about 2029 and have two or so years of thinking work being done by AI. If I plan it right I could get into the hands-on side of environmental work, like surveying and monitoring, before the robots catch up. It's still uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the degree and aim for the field side. I'd get a driving licence and a first-aid certificate, which employers on site always want. I'd keep the café job until graduation and save a bit, and I'd get to know the water authority's people through that placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to work with it. Five years is long enough to build something, and short enough that I can't be lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Book my driving lessons. It sounds small but half the field jobs ask for a licence, and my dad can't afford to teach me, so I'd pay for it from the café wage. It's a thing I'd regret not doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the field jobs get crowded because everybody has the same idea. If every graduate heads into hands-on work, there aren't enough places. I'd want something specific too, like water quality testing that needs a certificate.

say: Five years is a **window**, so we should set rules before it arrives.
I'd tell my flatmates to choose skills that are hard to automate.
think: I could reach the **hands-on** side of environmental work before robots catch up.
It's still uncertain, but I would graduate with a plan.
do: Stay on the degree and aim for **field** work.
Get a driving licence and a first-aid certificate.
Keep the café job and meet the water authority through a placement.
feel: Anxious but able to work with it, because five years is **long** enough to build something.
S3.quote: Half the field jobs ask for a licence, and my dad can't afford to teach me, so I'd pay for it from the café wage.
fieldNote: More time pushes Elena to buy specific, small credentials like a **licence** and a first-aid certificate.
She worries that everyone will have the same idea and crowd the field jobs.

steps.text: Book driving lessons and a first-aid certificate
Keep the café job through to graduation
Save a little each month for the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should stop panicking and use it. I'd still push for rules, because ten years is exactly how long governments take to do nothing. With friends I'd talk about what to study next, not whether to quit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be calmer. I'd finish my degree, get five or six years of real experience and have a chance to move into something that lasts. I might even do a master's in something like hydrology, which is mostly field and lab. I'd be uneasy rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd complete my degree, work for a few years in water monitoring and pay down the loan. I'd learn to use AI tools well, because by then everyone will. And I'd think about a postgraduate course in about 2030, once I knew where the work was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit of dread in the background, like knowing there's an exam coming. It doesn't stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your choices when there's a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the degree at normal pace and not rush into a job I don't like. I'd try one of the council contract jobs, even the short ones, because a few years of actual field experience matters more than any module. I'd also keep up the café shifts for a while, since they pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real plan for retraining that people can actually afford, and loan terms that don't punish graduates who change course. Ten years is plenty if it's used, and I'd keep asking them in public until they publish it.

say: Ten years is long, so we should stop **panicking** and use it.
Governments take about ten years to do nothing, so we must keep pushing for rules.
think: I'd be calmer, with five or six years of real **experience** before the big change.
A hydrology master's might be worth it.
do: Finish the degree and work in water **monitoring** for a few years.
Pay down the loan and learn to use AI tools well.
Decide on a postgraduate course around 2030, once I see where the work is.
feel: Mostly okay, with a bit of **dread** in the background like an exam to come.
S4.quote: A few years of actual field experience matters more than any module.
fieldNote: Elena becomes patient with a decade: **experience** first, postgraduate study later, once the work is visible.
Her one demand from government is affordable retraining and fairer loan terms.

steps.text: Take a short council contract job in water monitoring
Pay down the student loan with the first full wage
Learn the AI tools the water authority uses
Press the government for affordable retraining and fairer loan terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, no question. That's the one where my degree might be worth nothing before I finish it, and I'd have no time to move. It would help to have retraining that's free or cheap, loan repayments that pause, and some honest advice from the university about which courses will last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that students are treated as if our future is a problem to solve later. We're 19 and making huge decisions about debt right now, with almost no real guidance from anyone.

headlineQuote: We're 19 and making huge decisions about debt right now, with almost no real guidance from anyone.
portrait: Elena is a 19-year-old **environmental science** student sharing a flat, working at a harbour café and carrying a loan.
She is progressive and steady: she uses AI now and then, checks it, and wants rules on firms.
Her sharpest fear is that entry-level data work, the first job she was heading for, goes to AI first.
She answers each scenario with small credentials, such as a licence or first-aid certificate, and a lean towards hands-on field work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because her degree could be worth nothing before she finishes it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **retraining**, paused loan repayments and honest advice from her university about which courses will last.
